'I say to him/her', 'I told him' + quoted suggestion, repeated across a passage
description of the third person's responses in sequence (eyes closing, hand lifting, shoulders dropping)
setup line: 'imagine someone sitting in that chair', 'let me tell you how I'd hypnotize someone'
present tense narration of a session that is not, on its face, the listener's

not_this.why: the parent is any suggestion placed in a quote; this is a whole induction or sequence run on a stand-in
vicarious deepening uses a described person going under to deepen an existing trance; this uses the stand-in as the route for the suggestions themselves, often from a cold start
there the listener is asked to be the character; here the listener only watches someone else
covert induction is any induction framed as something else; this is one specific way of doing it

name: Challenge suggestion
summary: Suggest that something cannot be done, then invite the listener to try, so the failed attempt proves the suggestion.
cues: 'try to ...' + 'and find that you can't' / 'but you cannot'
'the harder you try, the more/less' placed inside or straight after an invitation to try
'go ahead and test it', 'test them and make sure they won't work'
'stop trying' shortly after
preceded by images of locking, gluing, freezing or forgetting

not_this.why: convincer is any staged proof of trance; a challenge is the specific try-and-fail wording, which most but not all convincers use
eyelid lock and the other convincer variants name the phenomenon; label the variant on the whole passage (install, test, release) and this entry on the try-and-fail sentence inside it
that claims resisting the whole process strengthens it; a challenge sets a single concrete test
reverse psychology instructs the opposite of what is wanted; here the speaker wants the attempt to fail and says so
a 'the harder you try, the...' line with no invitation to test a named inability is the comparative yoke, not a challenge

name: The more... the more
aliases: the more aroused the more you agree
summary: State that as one thing increases, another increases or decreases with it.
cues: 'the more ..., the more ...'
'the more ..., the less ...'
'the + comparative ..., the + comparative ...' ('the deeper, the better')
'more and more ... as ...'
first half names an ongoing act; second half names the response

not_this.why: the self-reinforcing loop is circular (A feeds B and B feeds A); this is a one-way yoke
contingent suggestion links occurrence to occurrence ('as', 'when'); this links amount to amount
cause-effect asserts 'X makes Y'; this asserts co-variation with a comparative
that labels a lone comparative with no standard ('deeper'); this pairs two comparatives
when the first term is resisting, fighting or trying not to respond, label that entry; this one covers every other pairing

name: Self-reinforcing loop
summary: State a circle: A increases B, and B increases A, so the state keeps feeding itself without further input.
cues: 'the more X, the more Y' followed by 'the more Y, the more X'
the same two terms appearing in swapped order in adjacent clauses
'round and round', 'feeding itself', 'a circle', 'a spiral', 'on and on'
'and that makes you ... which makes you ...' returning to the first term
'all by itself', 'without you doing anything' after a reciprocal pair

not_this.why: one-way link from one thing to another, with no return
the same ABBA shape as a figure of style, with no claim that the terms cause each other
says each accepted suggestion strengthens the others, not that two states feed each other

name: The harder you resist
summary: Declare that the effort of resisting itself strengthens the effect, so fighting it feeds it.
cues: 'the harder you try/resist/fight..., the...'
'every time you fight it'
'struggle all you like'
resisting or fighting as the cause of deepening

not_this.why: inevitability asserts certainty; this links certainty to the effort of resisting
the general comparative form; this is the case where the first term is resistance
resistance as participation calls resistance useful without claiming it backfires

name: Ratification
summary: Confirm a response the moment it happens, marking it as real and as the right thing.
cues: 'that's right', 'that's it', 'good', 'very good', 'just like that', 'there you go', 'perfect'
standalone short sentence following an instruction and a pause
'you felt that', 'there it is', 'you noticed'
ellipsis or line break before the phrase
repeats at regular intervals through a passage

not_this.why: that describes specific bodily signs as evidence of trance; ratification is the brief confirmation of any response
praise rewards the listener ('good girl', 'well done') to make the response more likely again; ratification marks the response as having occurred
naming the state says what the condition is called; ratification only confirms that something happened
a tag asks the listener to confirm; ratification is the speaker confirming

name: Pacing trance signs
summary: Describe the ordinary signs of settling, such as slower breathing and stillness, as evidence that trance is happening.
cues: named physiological signs: breathing slower, swallowing, eyelids fluttering, stillness, heavy limbs, face relaxing
perfect or progressive aspect marking a change that has occurred: 'has slowed', 'has become', 'are becoming'
interpretive clause: 'that is a sign', 'that tells you', 'that means you are going into trance'
noticing frames: 'you may notice', 'perhaps you've already'
the word 'sign', 'signal' or 'evidence' near a body description

not_this.why: ratification briefly confirms a response as it occurs ('that's right'); this entry names a sign of settling and presents it as evidence of trance
complex equivalence is the general claim that X means Y; when an ordinary bodily or behavioral sign of settling is presented as evidence of trance, use this narrower entry
sensation relabeling gives a felt sensation a new cause or meaning; when the meaning is simply that trance or relaxation is occurring, use this entry
a convincer stages a suggested phenomenon as proof; this entry interprets an ordinary sign of settling as evidence of trance

name: Apposition of opposites
aliases: as one hand rises the other sinks
summary: Pair two opposite experiences in one suggestion so each makes the other clearer and stronger.
cues: antonym pair in one sentence applied to experience: heavy/light, warm/cool, tense/relaxed, up/down, remember/forget
'as one ..., the other ...'
'while your X ..., your Y ...' with opposite predicates
left/right or body/mind assigned opposite states
parallel clauses differing mainly in the opposed terms

not_this.why: antithesis is a balanced contrast of ideas for effect; this suggests two opposite experiences at once
contrast shifts judgment by presenting a more extreme comparison first; here both sides are wanted responses
book and balloon is a specific convincer that uses this form; label the convincer when the test is staged
tense-and-release is a sequence of doing one then the other; apposition holds both together

that yokes any two amounts with 'the more..., the more/less'; label this entry only when the two halves are opposite experiences that are both being suggested, and both labels when such a pair is written in the comparative form

name: Question as suggestion
summary: Ask a direct question that the listener can only answer by having or checking for the response.
cues: direct question with a question mark addressed to 'you'
wh-words about experience: 'which', 'where', 'how much', 'how soon', 'what do you notice'
the question presupposes the response and asks only about a detail
followed by a pause, not by the speaker's own answer
the listener is not expected to reply aloud

not_this.why: the embedded question is wrapped in a statement ('I wonder which') and has no question mark
a rhetorical question makes a point and expects no inner search; this one needs the listener to check their experience
a loaded question forces a contested assumption about facts or character; this directs attention to a sensation or response
that is a request to act phrased as 'can you'; this is a question about experience
ask-and-answer has the speaker answer at once; here the answer is left to the listener

name: Suggestion repetition
summary: Give the same suggestion several times, word for word or in fresh words.
cues: the same suggestion content appearing three or more times in a script
a key phrase recurring verbatim at intervals
paraphrase runs: 'in other words', 'again', 'once more'
restatement immediately after a pause or a ratification
the suggestion returning in the closing passage

not_this.why: that repeats depth words to deepen trance; this repeats a content suggestion
a mantra is one short phrase repeated many times in a row as the activity itself
a refrain is a fixed line returning for structure; label refrain when the line is identical and placed at regular points
epizeuxis is a single word repeated with nothing between

name: Deeper and deeper
summary: Repeat depth words such as deeper, down, further, sinking many times through a passage, with no other mechanism.
cues: 'deeper and deeper', 'down and down', 'further and further'
high density of depth words (deeper, down, sink, drop, further) with no count or scene
'deeper still', 'even deeper', 'deeper now'
short sentences or fragments ending in a depth word

not_this.why: the general device of repeating any suggestion; this is its depth-word case, and takes both labels
labels 'deeper' when its comparison standard is omitted, even once; use this entry when depth words recur across a passage with no count, scene or contingency carrying them
a word repeated back to back as a figure; this is repetition spread across a passage
a repeated phrase or loop used to start trance

name: Compounding
summary: Tell the listener that each suggestion they accept makes the earlier and later ones stronger.
cues: 'each suggestion', 'every suggestion', 'everything I say' + 'stronger', 'easier', 'deeper'
'builds on', 'adds to', 'reinforces', 'locks in' applied to suggestions
'each time you follow/accept/respond' + increase
'the next one' + comparative
placed just after a response has been confirmed

not_this.why: compound suggestion is a sentence joining a true statement and a suggestion with 'and'; the names are alike but the devices are not
repetition restates a suggestion; compounding claims that suggestions strengthen one another
trigger strengthening says one trigger gains force with each use; compounding is about the whole set of suggestions
the self-reinforcing loop yokes two states to feed each other; compounding is about acceptance of suggestions

name: Giving a reason
summary: Attach 'because' and a reason to a suggestion, even a thin one.
cues: 'because', 'since', 'so that', 'which is why' attached to an instruction, request or offer ('close your eyes, because...', 'you can..., since...')
the causal clause gives grounds for doing or accepting the thing, not a mechanism by which a response happens
a reason that restates the suggestion or the obvious
'for the simple reason that'
instruction + comma + causal clause

not_this.why: if the 'because' clause explains why a response happens ('because you are sitting still, calm comes'), it is cause-effect; if it justifies an instruction, request or offer ('close your eyes, because there is nothing to look at'), it is reason-giving
values-linking ties the suggestion to something the listener cares about; label that when the reason is specifically their value
there the support is a cited source, not a 'because' clause
contingent wording links by time ('as', 'when'), not by justification

name: Sensory language
summary: Word the suggestion in concrete terms of sight, sound, touch, smell and taste so the listener simulates it.
cues: concrete sense words: warm, heavy, soft, bright, dim, hum, smooth, cool
body locations paired with a sensation ('across your shoulders', 'behind your eyes')
sensory similes: 'like warm water', 'like sun through a window'
verbs of perceiving: see, hear, feel, smell, taste
abstract state nouns are absent or immediately given a physical form

not_this.why: immersion is a passage with three or more senses within a few sentences, written to hold attention; with fewer senses, or inside a single suggestion, label this entry
nominalization is the opposite choice: an abstract noun the listener fills in
guided imagery leads through a scene step by step; sensory language is the vocabulary it is written in
sense crossing describes one sense in terms of another; this stays within each sense
that is the suggested phenomenon of a felt sensation; this is a way of wording any suggestion

name: First-person suggestion
summary: Write the suggestion with 'I' as the listener, so hearing or reading it is the same as saying it.
cues: 'I', 'me', 'my' referring to the listener in suggestion lines
short present-tense statements: 'I am', 'I feel', 'I can', 'my ... is'
lead-ins: 'say to yourself', 'the thought comes', 'you hear yourself think'
a section headed affirmations or written as a list of I-statements
second-person narration switching to first person for key lines
a second voice or track in 'I' running under a lead voice in 'you'

not_this.why: affirmations are first-person positive statements repeated as a practice; this is the pronoun choice wherever it occurs, repeated or not
repeat-after-me is the instruction to say the line; first-person wording is the form of the line said
inner-voice suggestion claims in the second person that the speaker's words become the listener's thoughts; this writes the thoughts directly
pronoun shift is the change of pronoun partway through as a device; this is sustained first-person wording
autogenic phrases are the specific heavy-and-warm formulae used as an induction

name: Affirmations
summary: Have the listener repeat positive first-person statements about themselves, usually in the present tense.
cues: first-person present-tense self-statements: 'I am ...', 'I can ...', 'I choose ...', 'I deserve ...'
positive wording with no negation
the same I-statement, or a short set of them, repeated
the word 'affirm' or 'affirmation'
an instruction to repeat daily or a set number of times
the classic formula 'every day, in every way ...'

not_this.why: any suggestion written in the listener's voice; affirmations are specifically positive self-descriptions that are repeated
a single 'you are X' or 'I am X' said as fact; label affirmation only when the I-statement is repeated or the listener is told to repeat it, and then both labels apply
first-person formulae about body sensations used as an induction, not self-evaluations

name: Breathe in, breathe out
aliases: breathing in calm, breathing out tension
in with the good, out with the bad
summary: Give the in-breath something to take in and the out-breath something to let go, so each breath carries a paired suggestion.
cues: 'breathe in X ... breathe out Y' with two different objects
'inhale' and 'exhale' each followed by an abstract noun (calm, tension, doubt, confidence)
'in with the ..., out with the ...'
'each breath in brings ...' paired with 'each breath out takes / carries away ...'
bare 'In, ... Out, ...' lines alternating a gain and a release
the pair repeated over several consecutive breaths

not_this.why: the deepener ties each exhale to going deeper and gives the inhale no content; this entry loads both halves with paired contents
the induction makes breathing the object of attention or guides its pace; it need not attach anything to the breath
apposition sets two opposite experiences side by side in any wording; here the opposites are mapped onto the two halves of the breath

name: Presupposition
summary: Phrase the sentence so it only makes sense if the target claim is already true.
cues: target response sits in a subordinate clause or noun phrase, not the main verb
the claim survives if the sentence is negated or turned into a question
definite or possessive noun phrase for a state not yet established: 'the heaviness', 'your trance', 'that calm'
cleft or pseudo-cleft: 'it's the ... that ...', 'what you'll find is ...'
no variant trigger carries the claim; if before/after/when, first/another/again, notice/realize, already/still/easily, begin/continue/stop or 'or' does, label the variant
a direct question (with a question mark) that carries the assumption is a loaded question, not this unit

not_this.why: an implication is inferred and can be denied; a presupposition is required by the grammar and survives negation
direct suggestion states the response as the main point
when the assumption rides on a direct question the listener is expected to answer, label loaded question; this unit covers statements
'I wonder how/when/which' is the embedded question; add a presupposition label only for the trigger inside it, by variant
a bind is the offer of options; presupposition is the mechanism that makes each option assume the outcome

name: Time-clause presupposition
summary: Put the wanted response inside a before, after, while, when or as clause, so the sentence treats it as something that will happen.
cues: 'before you ...'
'after you ...' / 'once you have ...'
'while you ...' / 'during ...'
'when you ...' / 'as you ...' followed by a response not yet established
'until you ...' / 'since you began ...'
wanted response in the time clause, minor instruction in the main clause

not_this.why: there the clause holds a fact already true and the main clause is the suggestion; here the suggestion is in the clause
a time bind offers a choice of when; a time clause offers no choice
an implied directive adds an internal response and a signal that it has happened

name: Ordinal presupposition
summary: Use first, next, another or again so the sentence assumes a series of responses, of which this is only one.
cues: 'the first thing you'll notice'
'which ... first' in a question or 'I wonder' clause
'next', 'the next time', 'second', 'last'
'another', 'again', 'once more', 'one more'
'also', 'too', 'as well' adding a response to one already named

not_this.why: 'still', 'already' and 'even more' comment on one response in progress; 'first', 'another' and 'again' count it as one of a series
'which first, left or right' adds listed alternatives; label both when alternatives are named
'again' alone stays here; label suggested memory when the script goes on to describe an earlier occasion that did not happen

name: Awareness predicate
summary: Ask the listener to notice, realize or become aware of the response, so its existence is assumed and only their awareness is in question.
cues: 'notice how/that ...'
'realize', 'discover', 'find that', 'recognize'
'be aware of', 'become aware that', 'are you aware'
'you may not have noticed yet ...'
'know that', 'remember that', 'it's nice to know that' followed by the target claim
awareness verb in the main clause, target response in its object clause

not_this.why: that names an observable sign and calls it evidence; this assumes the response and asks only for attention
mind reading claims knowledge of the listener's thoughts; this directs their attention to an assumed fact
'I wonder whether you notice' is an embedded question; label both when the object is an assumed response

name: Adverb / adjective presupposition
summary: Attach an adverb or adjective of manner, degree or attitude to the response, so the response is assumed and only its quality is open.
cues: 'how easily / quickly / deeply / completely you ...'
'already', 'still', 'yet', 'anymore' with a response verb
'even more', 'even deeper', 'so much more'
sentence-opening evaluative word: 'fortunately', 'luckily', 'happily', 'curiously', 'interestingly'
'it's interesting / nice / surprising how ...'
question or wonder-clause whose only open element is a manner or degree word

not_this.why: 'more relaxed' with no standard is comparative deletion; it need not assume a response is under way
'it's good to let go' is a value judgment with no judge; it does not assume the letting go is happening
'already' alone overlaps; label already-happened framing when the whole clause reports the effect as done

name: Change-of-state verb
summary: Use begin, continue, keep, stop or return with the response, so the sentence assumes the state that came before the verb.
cues: 'begin to', 'start to', 'starting to'
'continue to', 'keep', 'keep on', 'go on', 'carry on'
'stop', 'quit', 'no longer', 'not anymore'
'return to', 'go back to', 'resume'
'become', 'change into', 'turn into' with a state

not_this.why: that reports the effect itself as present or finished; a phase verb assumes only the state before it
'relax' asserts; 'continue to relax' assumes relaxing and instructs only its continuation
progressive tense is a tense choice; this needs a phase verb

name: Already-happened framing
summary: Speak of the effect as already under way or finished, so the listener's only task is to recognize it.
cues: 'already' with perfect or past tense: 'has already begun', 'you've already'
'it's done', 'that's settled', 'the decision is made', 'that change is made'
'all that's left is to ...', 'the only thing left is ...'
past or perfect tense for a response the script never requested
'somewhere back there', 'at some point', 'in the last few breaths' locating the effect in the session's past
'by the time you notice, it has ...'

not_this.why: direct suggestion states the response in the present or future ('your eyes are closing', 'you will relax'); this reports it in the past or perfect and leaves only noticing it
'continue' assumes a prior state; this states the effect itself as accomplished
inevitability says it will happen; this says it has
retroactive framing says the trait was always true, across the listener's life; this covers the session's recent past
future progression moves the listener to a later date to look back; this stays in the present

name: Loaded question
summary: Ask a question that cannot be answered, yes or no, without accepting an assumption built into it.
cues: direct wh-question ('how long', 'when did', 'what is it about', 'why do you') with a question mark
what it assumes is a wish, need, motive, history or trait of the listener, not a sensation they can check right now
'how much do you want ...', 'why do you keep coming back to ...'
'do you still ...', 'have you stopped ...'
no direct answer denies the assumption; denying it takes 'I don't' or 'it isn't'

not_this.why: label that when the question directs attention to a present sensation or response ('which hand feels warmer?'); label this when it assumes a wish, motive, history or trait
the same assumption in a statement is presupposition; loaded question needs a direct question the listener is expected to answer
'I wonder how long you've wanted this' owes no answer; label embedded question, with the presupposition variant for its trigger
a direct 'X or Y?' that offers two versions of the response is a bind, or a time bind when only timing differs; the or-presupposition variant covers alternatives inside a statement
a tag asks for agreement with a stated claim; a loaded question leaves the assumed claim unstated
a rhetorical question makes a point without seeking an answer; a loaded question solicits an answer that concedes its assumption

name: Implication
summary: Say one thing so that the listener infers another, and holds the inferred thing as their own conclusion.
cues: a limit on a permission or description: 'for now', 'so far', 'at first', 'for the first minute or two'
a ceiling that only makes sense if the response is coming: 'only as deep as', 'no faster than'
one statement about other people or about one option, with the application to the listener left unsaid
target response never stated as instruction or fact, and not named under 'don't' or 'not', anywhere in the span
the inferred claim can be named in a sentence and could be denied without contradiction ('I didn't say that')

not_this.why: a presupposition is required by the grammar and survives negation; an implication is inferred and can be cancelled
when the target response is named under 'don't', 'not' or 'won't', label negative suggestion, even with 'yet' or 'until'; implication covers inferences from sentences that do not negate the target
one statement with its application left open is implication; an unstated premise needs two stated parts (a rule and a case, or a reason and 'so') with the last step missing
indirect suggestion is the general style, covering story and possibility; implication is one specific inference left to the listener

name: If-then implication
summary: State a conditional whose 'if' is an easy act the listener controls, so doing the act counts as accepting the 'then'.
cues: 'if you [simple voluntary act], (then) you will / can [response]'
the 'if' clause names something the listener does on purpose, not something happening to them
the act has not been done yet; the sentence comes before it
the act is one the listener is about to do anyway: sit back, close the eyes, take a breath
ratification ('that's right', 'good') in the lines right after

not_this.why: its first half is already true or inevitable ('as you breathe out'); here the first half is a choice whose taking signals agreement
an implied directive has the internal response first and a behavioral signal after; here the act comes first and the response follows
'X means Y' asserts the meaning outright; label both when a conditional also says what the act means
that points back at something already done; this sets the meaning before the act

name: Unstated premise
summary: Give an argument with one step left out, so the listener supplies the missing premise or conclusion themselves.
cues: general statement followed by a particular case, conclusion left unsaid
'which tells you something', 'and you know what that means', 'you can work out the rest'
two stated parts of an argument (rule and case, or fact and pointer) with the last step missing from the text
a pause or line break where the conclusion would go
if the reason and the claim are both stated and joined by 'so' or 'because', label giving a reason

not_this.why: when the reason and the claim are both on the page, label giving a reason; label this only when a step, usually the conclusion, is visibly left for the listener
implication is one statement with an inference left open; this needs two stated parts of an argument with a step missing
when the stated fact is the listener's own act and the point is what they want or are, label your-actions-prove-it; add this label only if the conclusion is left unsaid
an unfinished sentence breaks off the grammar; here the sentences are whole and the logic has the gap
a cause-effect link asserts that X causes Y; this argues from X to Y through an unspoken rule

name: Assumed common ground
summary: Mark a claim as something speaker and listener already agree on, so it passes as a reminder instead of a new assertion.
cues: 'as you know', 'as you already know', 'as we both know', 'we both know'
'of course', 'obviously', 'naturally', 'clearly', 'needless to say'
'between us', 'as we agreed', 'you and I both know' presenting a claim as shared
'remember, ...' introducing something not said earlier in the script
'after all', 'as always', 'as we agreed' with no earlier agreement in the text
marker is an aside or sentence opener, or invokes shared agreement; the claim itself is stated in full

not_this.why: a truism really is undeniable; this dresses a contestable claim as already agreed
'you know / realize that X' with the claim as the verb's object is the awareness predicate; label this entry for an aside or opener ('as you know', 'of course') or a 'we' subject ('we both know')
mind reading claims knowledge of what the listener thinks or feels now; this claims they already hold a belief in common with the speaker
social proof cites what other people do; this cites agreement between speaker and listener

name: Nominalization
summary: Name a process or feeling with an abstract noun so the listener fills it with their own meaning.
cues: abstract nouns ending in -tion, -ment, -ness, -ance, -ity (relaxation, awareness, surrender, clarity)
noun forms of state or process words: comfort, peace, focus, trust, change, learning, understanding, control
'a certain ...', 'a sense of ...', 'a feeling of ...', 'that ...' before an abstract noun
abstract noun as object of have, find, discover, allow, enjoy
the noun could be replaced by a verb phrase ('your relaxation' = 'you relaxing')

not_this.why: there the process stays a verb with its manner left out; here it has become a noun
that gives the state a physical substance (fog, warmth); a nominalization stays abstract
that tells the listener what their present state is called; a nominalization only refers to a state loosely

name: Unspecified verb
summary: Use a verb that says something happens without saying how, so the listener does it their own way.
cues: process verbs with no manner or means: change, learn, experience, discover, understand, sense, become, allow, let go, drift, shift, settle
'in your own way', 'however it happens', 'somehow' following the verb
'begin to ...', 'allow yourself to ...', 'let yourself ...' plus a vague verb
no 'by ...' or 'with ...' phrase saying how the action is done

not_this.why: that turns the process into a noun; this keeps the verb and omits the manner
that states outright that the listener need not know how; this just leaves the how unsaid
deletion removes an object or topic from the sentence; here the verb itself is under-specified

name: Unspecified referent
summary: Talk about 'people', 'a person' or 'that feeling' without saying who or which, so the listener applies it to themselves.
cues: generic subject plus 'can' or 'may' plus a response verb: 'a person can', 'people can', 'one may', 'someone could'
'that feeling', 'this sensation', 'certain things', 'something' with no antecedent
'it' or 'this' with nothing earlier in the text to point to
a generic statement sitting between sentences addressed to 'you'
the sentence states a possibility, not a count or report of what others actually do

not_this.why: social proof reports what others actually do or feel ('most people find') as a reason to follow; here the generic subject is a stand-in for the listener and the sentence states a possibility
a truism is an undeniable general fact that asks for nothing ('everyone has felt tired'); this offers the wanted response under a generic subject ('a person can let go')
normalizing states that the response is ordinary and expected; this only leaves the subject open
that describes a specific third person responding in detail; this names no one

name: Comparative deletion
summary: Make a comparison and leave out what it is compared with: more relaxed, deeper, better.
cues: comparatives with no 'than' clause: deeper, more relaxed, easier, heavier, calmer, better, further
'more and more', 'even more', 'more deeply', 'less and less'
superlatives with no stated set: 'the best way', 'the deepest level'
'more' or '-er' adjective directly after become, feel, grow, get, go

not_this.why: that yokes two increases to each other; this is a single comparison with the standard missing

that is depth words restated across a passage; this is one comparative with no standard, on any quality. A run of 'deeper... deeper and deeper' takes the passage-level label, and a lone 'more comfortable' takes this one
'even more' and 'still deeper' also presuppose a prior amount; label that when the point is the assumed earlier state, this when the point is the open standard

name: Lost performative
summary: State a value judgment as plain fact, without saying whose judgment it is.
cues: 'it's good to', 'it's right to', 'it's important to', 'it's best to', 'it's wise to', 'it's wrong to'
evaluative adjective of worth or correctness (good, right, wrong, best, important, wise, natural) in an impersonal 'it is ... to/that' frame
'the best way to ...', 'the right thing is ...' with no one named as holding the view
no 'I think', 'for me', 'according to' attached to the judgment
the judged thing is a response or attitude the script wants, not a checkable fact

not_this.why: 'it's okay / all right / fine to' says the response is allowed and is permission-giving; label lost performative when the adjective asserts worth or correctness (good, right, best, important, wrong)
a free-standing 'that's right' or 'good' after a response confirms that it happened; a lost performative is a full sentence judging a response or attitude in general
a truism can be checked and is undeniable; this is an opinion presented as fact

name: Mind reading

name: Attributing feeling to things

name: Double meaning
summary: Use a word with two senses where both senses carry the suggestion.
cues: words with a literal and a trance sense: down, deep, under, drop, sink, fall, light, open, absorbed, follow, lost, blank

name: Pacing

name: Pacing and leading

'floating above', 'stepping out of', 'drifting up out of your body'
shift from 'you feel' to 'you see yourself feeling'

not_this.why: that changes how the body feels (numb, distant, not yours) without moving the viewpoint

name: Observer self

'a part of you that just watches', 'simply observing'
'at the back of your mind', 'from the edge', 'from a safe distance'
'while the rest of you ...' paired with a watching part
'without interfering', 'without judging', 'only noticing'

there the unconscious is addressed as a separate listener; here a watcher remains aware
that gives the analytical mind a decoy task so it stops monitoring; the observer continues to watch

name: It happens by itself
summary: Describe each response as happening on its own, so the listener experiences it as not done by them.
cues: 'by itself', 'all on its own', 'automatically', 'of its own accord'
'without you doing anything', 'you are not doing it', 'without any help from you'
'it just happens', 'it is happening'
body part or state as subject of a verb of movement or change, with no command: 'the arm lifts', 'the eyes close'
'that hand', 'the eyelids' in place of 'your' as the subject of such a verb (with distance or ownership words and no movement, it is body-dissociation)
'just watch it happen', 'notice it happening' said of a response in progress

not_this.why: that tells the listener they need not try or know; this frames a particular response as happening without their effort
puppeteering presents the speaker or the speaker's device as moving the body, even when a later sentence leaves that agent unstated; automaticity-framing presents the response as happening on its own
personification gives a body part or state wants, knowledge or a voice; here it moves or changes without a will of its own

name: Conscious / unconscious split

'your unconscious knows', 'already knows how', 'can learn', 'will take care of'

the same term for the second mind repeated across the passage as the addressee

that assigns the conscious mind a decoy job; the split assigns it nothing and speaks to the other mind
that tells the analytical part to rest or step aside; the split says nothing about the critic standing down
a part is picked out by a function ('the part of you that worries') and can be one of many; the unconscious is the one generic second mind, called by that name

name: Parts
summary: Address a part of the listener picked out by what it does, such as 'the part of you that worries', as if it were a separate person.
cues: 'part of you', 'a part of you that', 'that part'
'one part ... another part'
direct address to a part: 'I am speaking to the part that'
'thank that part', 'that part can rest', 'give that part a new job'
'come forward', 'step back' said of a part
'the side of you', 'the voice in you that' with a function attached

not_this.why: that addresses the unconscious as the one generic second mind; parts are picked out by specific functions and can be numerous
a persona has a name and traits of its own; a part is picked out by its function
when an analysing or checking part is only told to rest or step aside, label the bypass; parts-work addresses or negotiates with a functional part
that assigns the analytical mind a decoy task to occupy it; parts-work addresses or negotiates with a function-specific part
personification gives a body part, state or object a will; a part is a division of the self

name: Positive intention
aliases: what is this part trying to do for you
summary: Treat the part that objects or causes the problem as well-meaning, and ask or state what it is trying to do for the listener.
cues: 'trying to protect you', 'trying to help you', 'trying to do for you' said of a part, habit or feeling
'what does that part want for you', 'what is it trying to do for you'
'means well', 'has a good reason', 'on your side', 'not your enemy' said of a part
'positive intention', 'good intention', 'its purpose'
'thank that part for' followed by a protective aim
aim split from method: 'it wants you safe; it has just been going about it the hard way'

not_this.why: that calls the resisting itself part of the process; this credits the resisting part with a good motive and leaves the resistance as it is
the recipe contains this as one step, between signalling the part and generating alternatives; label this entry when the step stands alone
plain reframing gives a new meaning to an experience or event; this one always works through a part and its motive

name: Body detachment
summary: Suggest that a limb or the whole body feels distant, absent or as if it belongs to someone else.
cues: 'body asleep', 'the body sleeps while the mind'
'that arm', 'the body', 'those legs' replacing 'your', with a word of distance or ownership and no movement verb or outside vantage point
'far away', 'distant', 'as if it belonged to someone else', 'not yours'
'the body can rest without you', 'the body takes care of itself down there'
'you can no longer feel where your hands are', 'hard to tell where your legs end'
'only your mind remains', 'just a mind, just awareness'

not_this.why: that removes sensation from an area, usually to be tested; this removes ownership or nearness
that moves the viewpoint outside to watch; here the body recedes and the viewpoint stays
heavy or floating is still the listener's own body

name: Persona / alter
summary: Define a named alternate self with its own traits, presented as separate from the everyday self and able to take its place.
cues: a proper name assigned to a self other than the listener's own
'steps forward', 'comes out', 'takes over', 'switches in'
'you step back', 'you rest behind', 'you watch from inside'
trait list attached to the name: 'X is ..., X always ...'
paired switch cues: 'when you hear ...' and 'when I say ... you return'
third-person talk about the persona, then direct address to it by name

not_this.why: a role is played by the same self; a persona is presented as a separate self that replaces it
renaming gives the one self a new name; here two selves each have a name
a part is a function without name, traits or switch cue

name: Externalization
summary: Take a thought, feeling or the listener's will and place it outside them as an object or agent.
cues: 'outside you', 'out of you', 'in front of you' said of a thought or feeling
'give it a shape', 'a colour', 'a weight' followed by a location outside the listener
'set it down', 'put it down', 'hand it over', 'leave it there' said of an inner thing given physical form
'it is not you', 'something you have been carrying' when followed by placing it outside
an inner noun (worry, doubt, control) made into a physical object and placed outside the listener
'watch it drift away', 'watch it shrink' said of the object once it has a form outside the listener

not_this.why: that supplies the box or vault; externalization is the step of making the inner thing an outer object
there the state is a substance that fills, coats or drains through the body; label externalization when one discrete thing ends up outside the body and is set down, handed over or left
there the listener steps away from the experience; here the experience is taken out of the listener
personification gives a thing wants, knowledge or a voice; externalization is the move outside, and an externalized thing that then wants or speaks takes both labels

name: Six-step reframing
summary: Contact the part behind an unwanted behavior by signal, find its purpose, have it pick new ways to meet it, check for objections, and rehearse the change.
cues: 'the part of you that...' or 'the part responsible for X' addressed directly
a signal being set up and calibrated: 'let that signal get stronger for yes, weaker for no'
'what is it trying to do for you' / 'positive intention' / 'separate the behavior from the purpose'
'your creative part' asked for 'three new ways' or 'other choices'
'does any other part object?' / 'ecology check'
an imagined next occasion at the end, with the new behavior in place

not_this.why: that is any address to or negotiation with a part; this is the whole fixed sequence ending in an objection check
that is the single move of crediting a part with a good purpose, which is step three here
a reframe gives an experience a new meaning in a sentence or two; this is a procedure that changes the behavior, not a statement

name: Pronoun shift
summary: Change the pronoun used for the listener partway through, so the grammar itself separates them from who they were a moment ago.
cues: second-person passage followed by the same content in first person
'you' replaced by 'we' mid-passage
listener referred to as 'it' after earlier 'you'
announced switch: 'now say it as I'

not_this.why: object language is the content; a shift to 'it' is one way of delivering it
second-person narration keeps 'you' as protagonist without a switch
first-person suggestion uses 'I' throughout, including an 'I' voice running at the same time as a 'you' lead; a pronoun shift needs a switch point

name: Third-person self-reference
summary: Have the listener refer to themselves by an assigned term instead of 'I' and 'me'.
cues: 'no more I' / 'don't say I'
'say it as ...' + third-person sentence
listener speech lines using a name or 'this one' instead of 'I'
correction of 'I' to an assigned term

not_this.why: renaming assigns the term; this requires the listener to use it for themselves
first-person suggestion has the listener say 'I'; this removes 'I'

name: Repeat listening
summary: Tell the listener how often and for how long to listen or practice.
cues: frequency or timing phrases: 'once a day', 'every night', 'twice a week', 'come back tomorrow'
a stated course length or end point: 'for two weeks', 'until it feels automatic', 'then as needed'
a missed-day or review clause: 'if you miss a day', 'after a week, decide whether to continue'
appears in the description, pre-talk or the last lines before the wake-up

not_this.why: says future sessions will go faster and deeper ('each time you listen...'); a schedule says when and how often to listen and predicts nothing
assigns a separate action to carry out (an exercise, a report, an errand); a schedule only prescribes replaying or redoing the session itself
describes relistening as need or addiction; a schedule is a plain instruction
repeats the response many times inside one session, not across days

name: Habit stacking
summary: Attach the new behavior to something the listener already does every day, in a when-then sentence.
cues: 'whenever you [daily routine], you [behavior]'
'right after you ...', 'as soon as you ...', 'every time you finish ...'
first-person plan form: 'when I ..., I will ...', 'if ..., then I ...'
the cue is an ordinary routine: brushing teeth, pouring coffee, sitting down, getting into bed
the response is a deliberate action the listener performs, not a state that arrives by itself

not_this.why: also uses an everyday cue, but the response is framed as automatic and installed, not a plan the listener carries out
any suggestion for a later response; habit stacking is specifically an openly stated plan tied to an existing routine
links a response to something happening now in the session, not to a recurring cue in daily life

name: Drill
summary: Fire the cue, get the response, reset, and do it again many times in one session.
cues: 'again', 'once more', 'one more time', 'and again' repeated across a passage
three or more consecutive cue-response-reset cycles with near-identical wording
explicit practice language: 'let's practice', 'we'll do this ten times', 'another round'
numbered rounds: 'that was one', 'round three'
a reset instruction between firings: 'and come back up', 'open your eyes', 'let it go'
speed-up remarks: 'faster this time', 'quicker each time'

not_this.why: fires a cue once or twice as proof ('let's test that'); a drill is an extended block of cue-response-reset practice, often with counted rounds or 'again'
cycles between partial waking and renewed trance; a drill repeatedly fires and resets a named cue-response link. If both patterns are present, both labels can apply
repeats the suggestion's wording without firing and resetting the response each time

name: Mantra
summary: Repeat one short fixed phrase, or a fixed set of a few short lines, many times, spoken by the voice, by the listener, or by both.
cues: the same short fixed phrase, or the same few short lines in the same order, repeated as a sustained block, typically five or more times
one identical line recurring densely within a passage
'your mantra', 'chant', 'keep repeating', 'over and over'
repeated lines set as their own block or list
stage directions such as [mantra loops under voice] or [x10]

not_this.why: uses sustained repetition to lead into trance; label mantra as well when the same short fixed phrase forms a sustained repeated block
immediately repeats a word or short phrase, often just for emphasis; a mantra sustains a fixed phrase as a block, so a span can exhibit both
a line that returns at intervals through the script, not in a dense repeated block
repeats a suggestion a few times, often reworded; a mantra sustains fixed wording as a phrase
instructs the listener to say supplied words, even once; a mantra is the repeated phrase, whoever voices it, and both labels can apply

name: Repeat after me
summary: Tell the listener to say the suggestion themselves, aloud or silently, in words the writer supplies.
cues: 'repeat after me', 'say it with me', 'say these words', 'tell yourself', each followed by the line to be said
'out loud or in your mind', 'in your own voice', 'silently'
a quoted or set-off first-person line followed by a written pause or [pause for response]
a second-person instruction immediately followed by a first-person line
ratification right after the gap: 'good', 'that's right', 'again'

not_this.why: writes the suggestion as 'I' without instructing the listener to say it
has the listener state, write or sign a commitment to future conduct; if the writer supplies a promise to repeat, both labels can apply
asks the listener to supply the words or reasons themselves ('tell me why'); repeat after me supplies the words
asks only for a yes or a nod, not for the listener to voice the supplied content
repeats a fixed phrase many times by any voice; repeat after me is the instruction to voice supplied words, even once, and both labels can apply

name: Pairing
summary: Present a cue together with a state, again and again, so that the cue alone begins to bring the state.
cues: the same cue word or sound recurring right next to the same state description, three or more times
the cue dropped in as a bare word or sound between state descriptions, with no sentence saying what it does
'the word and the feeling', 'linked', 'connected', 'associated', 'tied together', 'go together', 'becoming one thing'
cue set off in quotes, italics or caps and followed by a ratifying state phrase ('there it is', 'that feeling again')
stage directions placing a sound effect at the moment a state is described

not_this.why: that states the rule ('when I say X you will Y', 'each time you hear X'); pairing just makes cue and state co-occur repeatedly and never says what the cue does

anchoring is an explicit capture step: the script builds or recalls one state and tells the listener to apply a cue 'as it peaks' or 'at its strongest'; label pairing when the speaker simply delivers the cue beside state descriptions, pass after pass, with no capture instruction
there the pleasant event follows something the listener did; here nothing is required of the listener

name: Pleasure pairing
summary: Pair a target word, act or idea with pleasure or arousal, so the target itself comes to feel good.
cues: 'X feels good', 'X is pleasure', 'it feels so good to X' repeated with the same X
pleasure or arousal words (good, warm, bliss, pleasure, tingle) adjacent to the target term in several consecutive sentences
equations of target and pleasure: 'obedience is pleasure', 'focus is bliss'
'X and the pleasure, together', 'that good feeling attaches to X', 'the feeling soaks into the word'
no condition on the pleasure (no 'when you do', 'because you', 'as a reward', 'you have earned')

not_this.why: reward arrives after and because of compliance; pairing has target and pleasure present together with no condition
that ties pleasure to trance depth; this ties pleasure to a target word, act or idea
that changes liking by pairing with already-valued things in general; this specifically uses a felt pleasure or arousal state

name: Evaluative conditioning
summary: Place a neutral thing next to things the listener already likes or dislikes, so it takes on their value.
cues: a target term repeatedly placed beside strongly valenced words or images without any argument linking them
lists that alternate the target with liked (or disliked) items
the target described in the company of warmth, home, safety, success, or of staleness, grey, cold
no causal or reward language ('because', 'when you do', 'earn')
the same target with a different valued companion each time

not_this.why: that pairs the target with a pleasure state felt in the moment; this pairs it with valued things and changes liking

that takes a cue with a definite existing reaction and holds a felt state against it to replace the reaction; label this when the target is only placed among liked or disliked things, with no state built or maintained and no old reaction named
reframing states a new meaning outright; evaluative conditioning never asserts anything, it only places things side by side
seeding makes an idea familiar for later use; this changes its value by its company

name: Second-order conditioning
summary: Pair a new cue with a cue that already works, so the response passes to the new cue.
cues: an already-installed cue fired in the passage, with a new cue presented at the moment its response arrives
old cue and new cue alternating in close succession ('settle, and press', 'chime, and blue')
'will do what X does', 'works just like', 'takes on the same power', said while X is being fired
'soon Y alone will be enough', 'you won't need X any more'
the original state is not built again; only the old cue is used to bring it

not_this.why: pairing joins a cue to the state itself; this joins a cue to another cue
installation states what the new cue does, even when it says 'Y now works like X'; label this only when X is actually fired in the passage and Y is presented with its response
chaining makes one trigger's response fire a different trigger; here one response is copied onto a second cue
stacking adds more responses to one cue; this adds more cues to one response

name: Counterconditioning
summary: Present a cue that brings an unwanted reaction while the listener is in an incompatible state, so the new reaction replaces the old.
cues: a feared or disliked cue introduced while a relaxed state is explicitly maintained
graded approach: 'from far away', 'a little closer', 'the next step', 'only as far as stays comfortable'
'still calm', 'stay relaxed as you picture ...', 'and the calm stays'
alternation between the difficult image and a return to relaxation or a safe place
'instead of the old feeling', 'where there used to be tension, now ...'

not_this.why: extinction shows the cue with no outcome and waits for fading; counterconditioning supplies an opposing response
that fires two installed anchors together; this brings the real problem cue into a prepared state
rehearsal has the listener imagine performing the future behavior; here the listener only holds the difficult image while a stated calm is kept, and the image is dropped when the calm slips
that only places a target among liked or disliked things; label counterconditioning when the cue has a named existing reaction and a felt state or sensation is held against it

name: Generalization
summary: Tell the listener the conditioned response also happens with similar cues, other voices or new settings.
cues: 'not only here', 'anywhere', 'wherever you are', 'in every part of your life'
'whether you hear it, read it or think it', 'in any voice', 'spoken or written'
lists of settings or cue forms each mapped to the same response
'just as well as', 'the same way', 'carries over', 'spreads into'
'eyes open as well as closed', 'awake as well as in trance'

not_this.why: discrimination narrows which cue fires the response; generalization widens it
that deliberately pairs one specific new cue with the old one; generalization extends to a class of similar cues or settings
a stated grant that a partner or other named people may fire a trigger is the shareable trigger; label generalization when the widening is over cue forms (heard, read, thought) or settings
future pacing rehearses one specific future moment; generalization asserts the range of cues and contexts
a bare 'always' or 'everywhere' is the quantifier; label generalization when it extends a conditioned response to new cues or settings

name: Discrimination
summary: Present a look-alike cue and let nothing happen, then present the true cue and let the response follow, so the response is trained to the exact cue.
cues: a contrast pair in the passage: a similar cue presented with no response, then the true cue with the response
the cue word spoken inside an ordinary sentence and followed by 'nothing', 'just a word', 'passes you by'
'that one ... and this one', 'you know the difference', 'feel the difference', 'not that, this'
two near-identical words, tones or sounds presented in alternation with different stated outcomes
the true cue fired straight after a non-response and ratified ('there', 'that is the one')

not_this.why: a condition that is only stated for a named trigger ('only in my voice', 'in conversation it is just a word') is trigger conditions; label discrimination when the look-alike is actually presented with no response and the true cue then fired
a stated limit on where the session's suggestions apply is scope limits; discrimination is the contrast presentation of cues, whatever its motive
extinction presents the trained cue itself with nothing following until it fades; here a look-alike gets nothing and the trained cue still gets its response
generalization widens the range of cues and settings; discrimination narrows it

name: Extinction
summary: Present the cue again and again with nothing following it, until the conditioned response fades.
cues: a known cue repeated with explicit non-response: 'nothing happens', 'nothing follows', 'you stay as you are'
'just a word', 'just a sound', 'an ordinary word again'
'fades', 'weaker each time', 'loses its pull', 'less and less'
the cue presented while alertness is stressed ('wide awake', 'eyes open')
a cue earlier followed by a state, now repeatedly presented while the passage marks its old response as absent

not_this.why: removal cancels the cue by declaration, and one later demonstration of non-response is still removal; label extinction when repeated presentations of the cue without its old response do the work
that pairs the cue with a new incompatible response; extinction presents it without its old outcome
satiation repeats a word until its meaning blurs; extinction repeatedly presents a previously effective cue without its old response
expiry sets an end time in advance; extinction is the repeated unpaired presentation itself

name: Positive reinforcement
summary: Right after the listener does what you want, give them something they want, so they do it again.
cues: instruction followed at once by a pleasant consequence
'because you ...', 'for doing that', 'as your reward'
'every time you ..., you get/feel ...'
'you've earned', 'that's what you get for'
reward wording that names the response it follows

not_this.why: pairing presents the good feeling alongside a cue whatever the listener does; reinforcement gives it only after a response

a contingent suggestion hangs the wanted response on something that is happening anyway ('as you breathe out, you relax'); in reinforcement the listener's own act is the condition and what follows is a payoff for it
ratification confirms that a response is happening and real; reinforcement adds a wanted consequence for it
negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant; positive reinforcement adds something wanted

name: Praise
summary: Say a short word of approval the moment the listener does the wanted thing.
cues: evaluation of a completed response: 'well done', 'you did that perfectly', 'you're doing so well'
approval of the listener: 'good boy/girl', 'I'm proud of you', 'I'm pleased'
'good' or 'very good' extended with what was done well: 'good, just like that breath'
approval placed immediately after the wanted response

not_this.why: ratification confirms the response is happening; praise judges the listener as having done well
labeling assigns a standing trait to get matching behavior later; praise rewards one response just made
affection flooding is heavy approval given up front, not contingent on any response

name: Pleasure as reward
summary: Suggest a burst of pleasant feeling that arrives the moment the listener complies.
cues: 'wave of pleasure', 'pulse', 'rush', 'glow' placed directly after a response
'because you ..., feel ...'
'every time you obey/follow/let go, it feels ...'
'your reward is', 'here it comes'
sensation wording that is conditional on an act, not free-standing description

not_this.why: pairing presents pleasure together with a word or idea, no response required; here pleasure is given for a response
the deepener ties pleasure to depth of trance, not to a specific act of compliance
a suggested sensation on its own is a phenomenon or proof; it becomes a reward only when made contingent on a response

name: Marker signal
summary: Use one brief, distinct sound or word to mark the exact moment the listener gets it right, with the reward to follow.
cues: stage directions: [click], [chime], [snap] placed immediately after a response
explanation of the signal: 'that sound means you did it right'
one fixed short word repeated after response moments, where the script has earlier defined it as a signal
an early passage pairing the signal with reward before it is used
the marked response precedes the signal; the reward may follow the signal

not_this.why: a sound trigger comes before the response and evokes it; a marker comes after the response and rewards it
praise carries approval in its meaning and varies in wording; a marker is one fixed signal whose value comes from pairing
ratification confirms a response in ordinary words; a marker is a trained signal backed by reward

name: Negative reinforcement
summary: Let the wanted response end something unpleasant, so the relief strengthens that response.
cues: 'the moment you ..., it stops/eases/drains away'
'as soon as you give in, the tension is gone'
'relief', 'release', 'let it stop', 'no more effort'
an unpleasant state described first, then ended by compliance
'it only gets easier when you ...'

not_this.why: punishment adds something unpleasant after an unwanted response to reduce it; negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to increase a wanted one
fear-then-relief uses the relieved moment to slip in a request; here relief is the consequence of the response itself
tense-and-release is a relaxation method using muscle contrast, with no contingency on compliance

name: Punishment
summary: Follow the unwanted response with something unpleasant, so the listener does it less.
cues: 'if you ..., then' followed by an unpleasant consequence
'you will be corrected', 'there are consequences', 'you'll regret'
extra work added after a named lapse: 'do it again', assigned lines or chores (nothing the listener holds is taken away)
suggested unpleasant sensation tied to a named lapse
scolding after a lapse: 'no', 'bad', 'wrong', 'I'm disappointed'

not_this.why: negative reinforcement increases a response by ending something unpleasant; punishment decreases a response by adding it
there the unwanted response only goes unrewarded; punishment adds something unpleasant for it
humiliation uses shame as emotional charge and need not be contingent on any lapse
fear of leaving attaches dread to stopping the relationship or practice, not to one specified response

name: Response cost
summary: After the unwanted response, take away something the listener values.
cues: 'you lose', 'I take away', 'is withdrawn', 'forfeit'
an accumulated total wiped: 'the streak goes back to zero', 'your points reset'
'minus', 'deduct', 'costs you'
privilege or permission revoked after a named lapse
the thing removed was given or earned earlier in the script or series

not_this.why: plain punishment adds something unpleasant or extra work; response cost removes something already held
time-out suspends the chance to earn or receive rewards for a stated period; response cost takes back a specific thing already earned
deprivation withholds in advance to raise a reward's value; response cost removes as a consequence of a lapse
extinction simply stops delivering the outcome; response cost takes back what was already given

name: Time-out
summary: After the unwanted response, shut off the listener's access to rewards for a short, stated period.
cues: 'for the next ten breaths / one minute / until I count to', attached to a named lapse
'no praise', 'no reward', 'nothing from me', 'you get nothing until'
'sit out', 'wait out', 'you wait', 'time-out'
'switches off', 'is paused', 'on hold' said of a pleasant state, with a stated return
'then it comes back', 'then we go on' closing the interval
a scripted silence framed as the consequence of a lapse

not_this.why: response cost takes back something already held (points, a streak); time-out removes the chance to receive anything for a period and takes nothing back
extinction stops rewarding one response with no end date and no announcement; time-out is a brief, bounded suspension of all reward after a lapse
deprivation withholds in advance to raise a reward's value; time-out withholds afterwards as a consequence
hot-and-cold withdraws warmth unpredictably to tighten attachment; time-out follows a stated rule, has a stated length and ends on schedule

name: Shaping
summary: Reward a small, easy version of the response first, then require a little more each time before rewarding.
cues: 'a little more each time', 'this time, go further before ...'
'that was enough before; now ...'
the same response requested in increasing size or duration, with reward after each
'first just ..., then ..., now ...' with praise between steps
explicit reference to an earlier, easier standard

not_this.why: the ladder relies on consistency with earlier agreements; shaping relies on a reward criterion that moves
graded escalation asks for more each time; shaping is the reinforcement of each approximation along the way
chaining links several different responses into a sequence; shaping refines one response

name: Intermittent reinforcement
summary: Reward the response only some of the time, unpredictably, so it keeps going when rewards stop.
cues: 'sometimes', 'now and then', 'not every time', 'you never know when'
'maybe this time', 'you'll have to keep going to find out'
repeated identical instruction where only some repetitions are followed by reward
praise or reward density that drops across a passage while the instruction continues
